body.text: In mid-October, Myanmar’s government released another round of low-resolution photos of Aung San Suu Kyi, the country’s detained former leader. She has been in prison since February 2021 – over five-and-a-half years.

On the morning of February 1, 2021, Aung San Suu Kyi was removed from power in a military coup, just hours before she was due to be sworn in for a second term as Myanmar’s de facto leader. She has been in the military’s custody ever since.

The military tried to justify her detention through legal maneuvers. In a series of separate trials from December 2021 to December 2022, Aung San Suu Kyi was sentenced to a total of 33 years in prison on charges of incitement, corruption, election fraud, and violation of Myanmar’s Official Secrets Act.

For more than five years, she had been mostly unseen by the outside world. Apart from photos released in April, August, and now October 2026, there was little news of her condition. Some – including one of her sons – questioned whether she was even still alive.

When the military releases photos of her, or permits a phone call, it is trying to address these concerns. Why did Myanmar suddenly care what the world thinks? Because the military is trying to push for diplomatic normalization after a transition to nominally civilian government. But the new government is led by the same man who led the 2021 coup: former military chief Min Aung Hlaing.

In December 2025 and January 2026, Myanmar’s miliary staged a heavily managed election that was widely boycotted by pro-democracy forces. To no one’s surprise, the party associated with the military won in a landslide. In April, Min Aung Hlaing was appointed president by a military-dominated parliament. Now the ex-general has the fig leaf of a democratic process to justify his rule.

And one of the first things Min Aung Hlaing did after becoming president was to move Aung San Suu Kyi from prison to house arrest. The authorities also reduced the length of her sentence. But Min Aung Hlaing has no intention of releasing her from prison, for both political and personal reasons.
